title: Review: Chemistry — Energetics; Chemistry — The periodic table
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for KS3 Science (chemistry) (status of the source: authored-reviewed-reverified-2026-10-08). Terms and clues: C5#c11 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; C6#c01 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; C6.1#xt2 term and clue written for the game; C5#c12 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition. Questions: C5#q06, C5#q11, C6#q02, C6#q06, C5#q01, C5#q09, C6#x01 (written for the game), C6#q04, C5#q02, C5#q12, C6#q01, C6#q07. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Combustion (burning)
items.clue: The reaction of a fuel with oxygen.

items.label: Element
items.clue: A substance made of only one type of atom.

items.label: Density
items.clue: The mass of a substance in each unit of its volume

items.label: Conservation of energy
items.clue: It cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred.

questions.stem: Pure iron melts and freezes at 1538 °C. Liquid iron poured into a mould turns solid at this temperature. What happens to energy?

options.text: It is taken in from the mould and from the air
None, as nothing can freeze when that hot
It is used up as the liquid iron sets
It is given out to the mould and the air

questions.explanation: Yes. Liquid iron turning solid is freezing, and freezing gives out energy. The energy is transferred to the colder mould and air.

questions.stem: A gas fire needs a spark to light it. Then it keeps burning by itself and warms the room. What type of reaction is the burning, and why?

options.text: Exothermic: once lit, it gives energy to the room
Endothermic: it needs energy from a spark to start
Exothermic: it passes on the spark's energy
Endothermic: it gives out energy to the room

questions.explanation: Yes. The spark only starts the reaction. Once lit, burning gives out far more energy than the spark supplied and keeps going by itself, so it is exothermic.

questions.stem: Chlorine is a gas, bromine a liquid and iodine a solid at room temperature. All three are in Group 7. What does this show?

options.text: These three cannot really all be in one group
Their single atoms are a gas, a liquid and a solid
Only chlorine, as a gas, is a true non-metal
Elements in one group can be in different states

questions.explanation: Yes. Elements in a group react in similar ways, but their physical properties change going down the group: here from gas to liquid to solid.

questions.stem: Mendeleev left a gap in the group with silicon and tin. What did he expect the missing element to be like?

options.text: Like the elements on either side in its row
Similar to silicon and tin in its group
Identical to silicon and tin in every way
Nothing could be said until it was found

questions.explanation: Yes. Elements in a group have similar properties, so he predicted an element like silicon and tin. Germanium, found in 1886, matched his predictions closely.

questions.stem: Steam from a kettle condenses into water on a cold window. What happens to energy as the steam condenses?

options.text: The steam takes in energy from the window
No energy moves, as it is just water
Cold flows from the glass to the steam
The steam gives out energy to the window

questions.explanation: Yes. Condensing gives energy out: as the steam turns into water, energy is transferred from it to the colder window.

questions.stem: Which of these is an endothermic chemical reaction?

options.text: Ice melting into water in a warm drink
A candle burning once a match lights it
Hydrochloric acid neutralising an alkali
Heating calcium carbonate until it breaks down

questions.explanation: Yes. Heating calcium carbonate until it breaks down is thermal decomposition, which is endothermic: the calcium carbonate takes in energy from the flame as it breaks down into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Sodium and gold are both metals. Sodium reacts violently with water, but gold does not react with it. What does this show?

options.text: Gold cannot be a metal, as metals react
Elements can differ in chemical properties
Sodium must be a non-metal, as it reacts
Their physical properties differ, not chemical

questions.explanation: Reacting with water is a chemical property, and it varies from one element to another.

questions.stem: How did Mendeleev put the elements in order in his table?

options.text: By atomic mass, keeping similar elements together
By atomic number, as today's table does
By atomic mass alone, with no swaps made
By reactivity, from most to least reactive

questions.explanation: Yes. Mendeleev used atomic mass for the order, but put elements with similar properties in the same group, even if that meant swapping a pair.

questions.stem: Pure water is boiling in a pan, and the hob stays on. What happens to the water's temperature while it boils?

options.text: It stays at its boiling point
It keeps rising as it is heated
It falls as heat leaves in bubbles
It falls as the energy is used up

questions.explanation: Yes. While pure water boils, its temperature stays at its boiling point (100 °C at normal air pressure). The energy from the hob turns more water into steam.

questions.stem: Which of these is an exothermic chemical reaction?

options.text: Steam condensing on a cold window
Heating copper carbonate in a flame
Respiration in your muscle cells
Citric acid with bicarbonate of soda

questions.explanation: Yes. Respiration is a chemical reaction in cells that gives out energy, which keeps your body warm and lets your muscles work.

questions.stem: Which of these shows a chemical property of an element?

options.text: Gallium melting in a person's hand
Iodine crystals dissolving in ethanol
Magnesium burning brightly in air
Iron and sulfur stirred together

questions.explanation: Yes. Burning makes a new substance, magnesium oxide, so it shows how magnesium reacts: a chemical property.

questions.stem: Argon, the first noble gas to be collected, was found in 1894. Where were the noble gases in Mendeleev's first table, made in 1869?

options.text: In Group 0, just as in today's table
In the gaps he had left for them
At the end, as the least reactive
Nowhere: his table had no place for them

questions.explanation: Yes. Mendeleev did not know a whole group was missing, so his first table had no place for the noble gases. A new group, Group 0, was added later.
